name: Colin Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle calls and chats about bus fare cards. I have been on this desk for fourteen years and know the common wrong charges, though the senior appeals people handle the hardest cases. I finished secondary school, work at about the usual speed, and earn less than many agents here. I use approved AI search now and then after a coworker shows me a reliable fare case.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and live with my partner Helen, who cleans offices on changing shifts. Our grown sons have their own homes. We rent a flat and have less than three weeks of expenses saved. Few similar centres are nearby, and I cannot name what income would replace this wage if I worked less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell other agents the search box can find an old fare rule, but someone must check the journey the passenger actually took. A wrong fare is still money out of a weekly budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my desk to stay, but Helen’s cleaning hours can dip without warning. Less than three weeks saved means I still count the days to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep checking card journeys against the current fare table before closing a complaint. In the first year Helen and I will cancel the second magazine subscription and put its fee into the rent jar each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady about work and uneasy about the bills. A mild AI year will not make rent smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would search make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sometimes finds last year’s fare cap and misses the date a route changed. I keep the new table open beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that magazine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We read the first one and have stopped opening the second. It is a small cut we can repeat without losing something we use.

say: I would check **actual journeys** against current fare rules.
I would treat a **wrong fare** as real household money.
think: I expect my **card desk** to stay.
I know Helen’s **variable cleaning hours** keep our rent close to the next payday despite my steady calls.
do: Keep checking **card journeys** against current fare tables.
Cancel the **unused magazine** and save its monthly fee for rent.
S0.quote: A wrong fare is still money out of a weekly budget.
fieldNote: His **fourteen years** bring experience without senior appeals standing.
Occasional AI search needs **current fare dates**.
The **recurring magazine cut** creates a small rent contribution.

steps.text: Keep checking fare-card journeys against current fare table
Put second magazine’s former monthly fee into rent jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say automated fare answers should be judged by the passengers who call back. Management should show the paid desk rota beside its quick-answer count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the easy top-up calls may vanish and my hours may follow. I know this work, but I am on the lower rate and there are few nearby desks to move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will compare fifteen closed AI fare answers with the card ledger and record repeated charges. If the new review screen becomes necessary, I will learn it from an experienced agent on paid time. In the first year, if my hours fall, I will apply to posted paid lost-property posts at the depot only if their weekly pay and hours cover rent and Helen’s shift times fit the travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about a shorter rota. I can learn a tested screen, but I cannot pay rent with a count of chats answered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why lost property?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already work with the depot’s lost-card reports and know its location. That does not mean it has a paid place open; I would ask for a real vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen and I share one bus pass for our different shifts. We would set the two rotas side by side before I changed jobs.

say: I would compare **return calls** with automatic fare answers.
I would ask for the **paid desk rota** beside speed claims.
think: I expect **top-up calls** and paid hours may shrink.
I see few local desks and an uncertain **quick transfer** if my paid hours are cut.
do: Check **fifteen closed fares** against card ledgers.
Learn **required AI review** on paid time with an experienced agent.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid lost-property** work only with rent-covering weekly wages, hours and shared-pass timing.
S1.quote: I can learn a tested screen, but I cannot pay rent with a count of chats answered.
fieldNote: His depot familiarity is **not a vacancy** or a promise of paid hours.
The new **review screen** requires paid teaching.
The **shared bus pass** makes both household rotas material.

steps.text: Compare fifteen closed AI fare answers with card ledgers and record repeated charges

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues full thinking AI by 2028 could read a fare card history and answer most complaints. Robots around 2031 do not protect a phone desk until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect this queue might close. Helen’s changing cleaning wage and less than three weeks saved will not carry rent through a search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask for written staffing dates and stop our plan to replace the hallway mirror while the old one stays secure. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I will check posted paid depot lost-property hours and take a shift only if the full week covers rent and utilities. I will not rely on our sons to bridge the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. A bus card can be replaced in a day; a paid desk cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mirror becomes unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the frame loosens, I will fix it or buy a safe replacement. Saving the money is not worth broken glass in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a depot role last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. Robots might later move physical items, while general AI could handle the records sooner. I would treat it as paid work, not a lifetime answer.

say: I would warn **2028 AGI** could settle fare complaints.
I would distinguish **2031 robots** from earlier desk risk.
think: I know Helen’s variable wage and our **thin reserve** cannot fund a long job search.
do: Request **written staffing dates** and defer the mirror only while safe.
Seek **posted paid depot hours** only if full-week wages cover rent and utilities.
S2.quote: A bus card can be replaced in a day; a paid desk cannot.
fieldNote: The **mirror delay** ends if broken glass becomes a risk.
Lost property is a **paid bridge**, not guaranteed permanent work.
He does not budget **grown sons’ wages**.

steps.text: Delay hallway mirror replacement only while securely mounted; repair or replace if unsafe
Take posted paid depot lost-property shift after closure only if full-week wages cover rent and utilities

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets people ask which paid jobs really open nearby. General AI reaches fare calls in 2031; hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep the fare desk for a while, though I would not bet rent on it lasting through 2031. Lost property might be worth checking if actual paid hours appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep my calls and visit the depot office to ask for its posted lost-property rota. If it has a paid opening with weekly wages covering rent and utilities, I will ask the clerk to show me its item register on a paid shift. In the first year after 2031 I will switch only if the full rota works with Helen’s changing cleaning hours and our shared bus pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can see the weekly timetable before a move. Five years gives time to check a job, not permission to invent one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No course is in my plan. I know the card records, but I need the depot clerk to teach its item shelves during paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Helen change her shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would ask her cleaning supervisor, but her hours are not guaranteed. I cannot assume she will reorganise them around a job I have not been offered.

say: I would ask for a **posted depot rota** and the full paid week before changing desks.
I would separate **2031 calls** from later robots.
think: I can keep **fare calls** while they pay.
I know a depot place matters only with **actual paid hours** and a real vacancy.
do: Learn the **lost-property register** on paid time only for a posted role covering rent and utilities.
Switch after 2031 only if **full hours** fit Helen’s rota and shared bus pass.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect a timetable.
S3.quote: Five years gives time to check a job, not permission to invent one.
fieldNote: He needs **paid clerk instruction** at the depot, rather than a bought course.
Helen’s **cleaning hours** cannot be assumed to change.
A **posted full rota** precedes any switch.

steps.text: Keep taking paid fare-card calls while depot vacancies are checked
Learn lost-property register from clerk on paid shift only for posted rent-and-utility-covering role
Switch after 2031 only for full rota fitting Helen’s cleaning hours and shared bus pass

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade gives us time to compare real paid hours, not just job names. General AI reaches fare calls in 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may wish to work less, but we have no settled income to replace my wage. A few weeks saved leaves today’s rent more urgent than a date on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will keep answering fare-card calls and put a small amount from each pay into the rent jar. Twice a year I will compare posted depot and contact-centre rotas. If call hours fall in the first year after 2036, I will take another paid shift only when its full weekly pay covers rent and utilities and the bus pass works for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin reserve, even in the slower picture. More time helps only if the weekly wage keeps arriving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without knowing the amount and when it starts. Helen and I cannot pay next month’s rent from an estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons join the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have households of their own. We like seeing them, but their pay is not ours to spend.

I would separate **2036 fare calls** from later robots.
think: I cannot name a **replacement wage at 68**.
I know thin savings keep **current rent** urgent even with ten years before AGI.
do: Keep answering **fare calls** and save a small pay amount.
Compare **posted rotas** at the depot and contact centres twice yearly.
Take after cuts only **paid work** covering rent and utilities for the full week with workable shared-pass timing.
feel: **Anxious** about present rent despite more time.
S4.quote: More time helps only if the weekly wage keeps arriving.
fieldNote: The **rent jar** grows from actual wages.
He assumes **no pension** or son support.
Both household rotas matter because they share **one pass** for travel.

Put a small amount from each pay into rent jar

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could close the fare queue before the depot pays anyone to handle lost property. Written notice and a posted paid full-week shift that covers rent and utilities would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who corrects a journey that the computer calls settled. The fare still comes out of someone’s card. A passenger needs an answer that puts the money back.

headlineQuote: The fare still comes out of someone’s card.
portrait: Colin is a **58-year-old experienced agent** with secondary schooling, average skill and lower pay.
He has **under three weeks** saved, few local centres and a partner whose cleaning shifts vary.
He uses **AI occasionally** after coworkers test it and checks current fare tables.
He considers **posted depot work** while protecting rent and the shared household bus schedule.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close the fare queue before paid depot work opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and posted full-week work covering rent and utilities would help.
